Chapter 8: Handling Guilt, Regret, and Unmet Expectations
Let’s face it—guilt and regret are feelings we all know too well, especially when life throws its toughest challenges our way. Have you ever noticed how these emotions often creep in when there’s a gap between what you wish you could do, and what’s actually possible?
Sometimes, the pressure to meet impossible standards—whether they come from ourselves or from people around us—can lead to that heavy sense of self-blame and disappointment.
But here’s something worth thinking about: not all guilt, or regret, is created equal. Some of it can actually help us grow, while some just weighs us down for no good reason.
Try asking yourself, is this useful guilt—a clear signal that maybe I need to make a change or fix something? Or is it useless guilt, based on standards no one could realistically meet, or stuff that’s just out of your control? The same goes for regret. Sometimes it teaches. Other times, it traps.
So, what can you actually do with these tough feelings?
Here are a few gentle strategies that might help:
First, reality-check your standards. Are your expectations even possible, or are they fueled by perfectionism or wishful thinking?
Next, if you realize you’ve really hurt someone, own up to it. Make amends if you can, try to repair the harm—and then, give yourself permission to move on.
It’s just as important to forgive yourself for being human. We all make mistakes. We all have limits. That doesn’t make you unworthy—it just makes you real.
And when your mind keeps dragging you back to the past, see if you can gently redirect your energy to what’s right in front of you. What can you do now, instead of replaying old scenes over and over?
Here’s a real-world example: picture a parent who feels guilty about losing patience with their child. Instead of beating themselves up, they could apologize, make a plan to handle it better next time, and then let themselves move forward. Getting stuck in guilt only saps your hope—and your energy.
Or think about someone who regrets a career choice. Sure, it’s natural to wish some things had gone differently. But instead of turning regret into a weapon, they could look at what they’ve learned, tweak their plans for the future, and remind themselves that no path is perfect.
At the end of the day, guilt and regret don’t have to be lifelong sentences. If you treat them as signals—like helpful nudges instead of harsh judgments—you’ll find it’s a lot easier to let go of the endless “shoulds” and focus on living your real life, as well as you possibly can, right now.
